title: Evaluate
summary: Pick the question whose answer would decide whether the argument holds. Test each choice with two answers: one should help, the other should hurt.

slides.title: The question that settles it
body: Evaluate answers are questions or pieces of information to look up. The right one targets the gap: depending on how it is answered, the argument gets stronger or weaker.
A choice whose answer wouldn’t matter either way is wrong, however interesting it sounds.
slides.callout: Answer the question both ways. If one answer helps and the other hurts, you’ve found it.

slides.title: How you’ll see it
stems: The answer to which one of the following questions would be most useful in evaluating the argument?
Which one of the following would it be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
In order to evaluate the argument, it would be most helpful to determine which one of the following?

steps.label: Find the gap
steps.do: Same as weaken and strengthen: what does the argument take for granted?

steps.label: Predict
steps.do: Phrase a question about that assumption: did anything else change? Is the sample typical?

steps.label: Answer it both ways
steps.do: For each choice, imagine a yes and a no. Does one help the argument and the other hurt it?

steps.label: Drop the neutral ones
steps.do: If neither answer changes how strong the argument is, the choice is out.

slides.title: Worked example
slides.stimulus: Since the town of Ferris lowered the speed limit on Route 9 from 55 to 45 miles per hour, the number of accidents on Route 9 has dropped by a third. The town council concludes that the lower speed limit made Route 9 safer.
slides.stem: The answer to which one of the following questions would be most useful in evaluating the council's conclusion?

choices.A: Do most drivers in Ferris approve of the lower speed limit?
choices.B: How many miles long is Route 9?
choices.C: Did the amount of traffic on Route 9 fall during the same period?
choices.D: Are speed limits on other roads in Ferris also 45 miles per hour?
choices.E: Has the town council lowered speed limits on other roads in the past?

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.note: The lower limit made the road safer: a causal claim.
steps.highlight: the lower speed limit made Route 9 safer

steps.label: Gap
steps.note: Fewer accidents could have another cause, like less traffic.

steps.label: Answer C both ways
steps.note: Yes, traffic fell: the drop may be due to fewer cars, so the argument weakens. No: the drop is more likely due to the limit, so it strengthens.

steps.label: Check the rest
steps.note: Approval, road length, other roads and past decisions don’t change the strength of the argument however they are answered.

why.A: Approval doesn't bear on whether the road became safer.
why.B: Length is the same before and after, so it doesn't explain the change.
why.C: Correct. A yes weakens the causal conclusion; a no supports it.
why.D: Other roads' limits don't explain what happened on Route 9.
why.E: The council's history doesn't affect whether this change worked.

slides.title: Cheat card
lines: Find the gap first, as for weaken and strengthen.
Answer each choice yes and no.
One answer helps, the other hurts: that’s the one.
